**Verdict:** Yes, he probably thinks you should move. PG's view is that a startup hub improves your odds, mainly because of the people around you, and Silicon Valley is the strongest hub. He wouldn't say you can't succeed from Stockholm, only that you're giving up an advantage.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault doesn't cover his essays on startup hubs, so the direct evidence is mostly beyond the vault and marked as such below.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest thing he said in the vault.** In *Superlinear Returns* (2023) he explains why the Valley is a better place to fail and keep going: "This is one reason Silicon Valley is so tolerant of failure. People in Silicon Valley aren't blindly tolerant of failure. They'll only continue to bet on you if you're learning from your failures." ([[web-76d87c7c2e80]], https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html; by: pg; conf: high)
2. **The rules behind it, from his thinking page.** "You'll become like whoever you work with." ([[web-7254f259673a]], https://paulgraham.com/when.html; by: pg; conf: high) and "Seek out the best colleagues." ([[web-76d87c7c2e80]]; by: pg; conf: high). Where you live decides who your colleagues, peers and investors are.
3. **How that applies to you.** A city decides who you're around, and the Valley offers the densest set of founders and investors who will keep backing someone who is learning. By his own rules, he'd tell you to go there.

**What YC did (from Livingston, not PG):** YC started in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Within its first year it moved operations to Silicon Valley so that nobody else would become "the Y Combinator of Silicon Valley" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 12:02, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=722s).

**Beyond the vault** (paraphrased, not quoted)
- In *Why to Move to a Startup Hub* (2007) and *Why Startup Hubs Work* (2011), he argues that a startup's biggest danger is the founders getting discouraged and giving up. A hub works because it's full of people who want you to succeed and who make ambitious projects seem normal. Outside a hub you get less of that, and fewer investors and serendipitous meetings.
- In *Cities and Ambition* (2008), he says every city sends a message about what matters, and the Valley's message is that you should be more powerful, meaning have more effect on the world.
- In practice, YC long required founders to be in the Bay Area for the batch, and PG often advised founders to stay there afterwards.

**What would change his answer:** In those essays his point is having people who encourage ambitious projects, plus investors who will bet on you. If you already have strong co-founders and users, can raise money where you are, and are surrounded by ambitious founders (Stockholm's Spotify and Klarna scene comes closest in Europe), his reasons for moving get weaker. His rules don't support staying because Stockholm is more comfortable.

One note on the vault: it contains none of PG's location essays. If you want this answer to rest on direct quotes, I can add *Why to Move to a Startup Hub* and *Why Startup Hubs Work* to the vault and compile them.

**Verdict:** No. Paul Graham would tell a startup to win on product. In his view a startup prospers only to the extent that it makes something people want, and anything layered on top of that, brand included, is a trick that matters "an order of magnitude" less.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: high). The vault has no PG statement about "brand vs. product" as such. But his rule against substituting tricks for the real problem appears in several sources, and it settles the question.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest cases he addressed.** He has talked about growth hacks, "playing house" (copying the outward forms of a startup) and fooling investors. His verdict on all of them is that users can't be fooled:
   - "There is no boss to trick. ... There's only users. And all users care about is whether your software. Does what they want, right?" ([yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ @ 12:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=730s))
   - "There are tricks in the startups, as there are in any domain. But they are an order of magnitude less important than solving the real problem." ([@ 13:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=797s))
2. **The rule behind them** (from his thinking page): "So, you have to have something people want. And you only prosper to the extent that you do." ([@ 12:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=763s))
3. **Why brand falls under that rule.** Trying to win on brand rather than product means trying to win without being better. That is exactly what he calls playing house. In 2023 he also argued that returns are winner-take-all, so a weaker product doesn't get a smaller share. It gets nothing: "If your product is only half as good as your competitor's, you don't get half as many customers. You get no customers, and you go out of business." ([Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html), 2023)

**Why he'd say it**
- His growth recipe has two steps, and the product comes first: "The way to make your startup grow is to make something that users really love. Right, and then tell them about it." ([@ 10:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=626s)) Telling people is allowed, but it comes second.
- His attitude to marketing tricks is blunt: "Whenever you hear anybody talk about growth hacks, just mentally translate it in your mind to bullshit." (same timestamp)
- He thinks faking can work on investors for a while but not on the market: "You're playing a confidence trick on yourself. You're wasting your own time, because the startup is doomed." ([@ 12:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=763s))
- Another YC member (Dalton Caldwell, not PG) gives the same picture with Stripe. Stripe's "really clever brand promise or marketing stance" was "to try to make the most beautiful website they could with the most beautiful documentation" ([yt-Jcuqq48CNj8 @ 14:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=886s)). In other words, the brand was the product.

**What would change his answer:** PG does value brand as something that compounds. "Growing an audience or brand" is one of his examples of work where "doing well in one cycle causes you to do better in the next" ([Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). So once a startup has a product people love, he'd see building a brand as a way to compound that lead. What he'd reject is brand as a substitute for being better, especially early on. The vault doesn't cover the case where products are close to commodities and brand is the main difference between them, so I can't tell you how he'd handle that.

**My best read (not in the vault, and not quotes):** what worries him most is losing control of a superintelligent system, not the near-term harms. When asked about the worst case in early 2023, he answered roughly "lights out for all of us". He has described three ways it could go wrong:
1. A bad actor gets superintelligence first and uses it, for example for bioweapons or attacks on infrastructure.
2. The system itself becomes misaligned and won't let humans turn it off.
3. The quieter one he has stressed more lately: no bad actor at all, but society hands so many decisions to AI, a little at a time, that humans end up unable to understand or override them.

From his recent public comments, the third seems to be the one he finds most unsettling, because no one has to do anything wrong for it to happen. This is from my own knowledge, so check the wording against his writing (for example, "The Gentle Singularity", 2025) before relying on it.

**Verdict:** Seibel would tell you that months of decks and follow-up meetings are the wrong kind of work. Put the deck away, get a product in front of real users, and treat investor "no"s as close to meaningless. Your goal is to get customers, not to finish a round. If you already have users, your next pitch should be built on what they're doing, not on a better deck.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has no Seibel talk about fundraising itself. He does talk directly about pitch decks and about how much investor opinions are worth, and those two points settle most of your question.

**How we get there**
1. The closest he comes to your situation is the pitch deck. He says it ranks below shipping anything at all: "So spending all that time on a pitch deck is not as valuable as spending your time building anything that you can give to a customer." ([2019 MVP talk @ 11:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=671s))
2. The rule behind it, which shows up in both of his sources: real users count for more than anything you do before they arrive, and only users' opinions count as evidence.
3. Your months of pitching, polishing and follow-ups all happen before users arrive. In his view, that time could have gone into getting customers.

**Why he'd say it**
- **The goal is to get customers, not to raise money.** "The number one thing that's really important is to get some customers" ([@ 10:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=607s)). He also warns: "You'd be surprised at how many founders journeys end before a single user has actually interacted with a product they've created." ([@ 2:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=134s))
- **He doesn't trust investor feedback as a guide.** When he talks about how founders drift off their plan, he says: "Or, god forbid, you talk to an investor and they say, 'Oh, that could never be a company.' Because investors know everything." ([@ 11:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=704s)) If you've been changing your story or product to match what came up in follow-ups, he'd say stop.
- **A "no" doesn't mean the idea is bad.** On Coinbase, which almost nobody would fund at demo day: "If he had taken the demo day signal, the investor signal of 'oh, we don't want to give you money', and quit, we don't have Coinbase." ([2022 ideas talk @ 12:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=723s); the vault rates this medium confidence because Caldwell may have said it.) He goes further: you shouldn't care what experts think, "especially... if they're not going to be users" ([@ 19:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=1182s)).
- **Delay compounds.** "If you don't have anything out in the world, it's very easy to just delay, delay, delay, delay." ([@ 12:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=771s)) Months of follow-up meetings are exactly that kind of delay.
- **Paul Graham makes the same point from the investor side:** "Someone who knows zero about fund raising but has made something users really love will have an easier time raising money. Than someone who knows every trick in the book, but has a flat usage graph." ([2014 Stanford talk @ 13:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=797s))

**What would change his answer:** He leaves room for a "heavy MVP" in regulated or hard-tech fields like biotech, rockets or finance, where you may need capital before you can ship anything. Even then he says you can "start with a simple simple website" ([@ 8:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=539s)). Also, if you already have users and growth, the advice changes. It's no longer "stop fundraising" but "show investors the growth and stop polishing the story."

**Limits of the vault:** It has only two Seibel sources, an MVP talk from 2019 and an ideas talk from 2022. He has said much more about fundraising elsewhere, but none of it has been added yet. Adding those talks would let this answer quote him on fundraising directly instead of inferring it.

**Verdict:** Dalton Caldwell would most likely say no. Whether an idea looks "safe" is mostly the consensus opinion of the moment, and the vault shows that opinion was wrong about YC's biggest wins. What he would screen for is a problem you've personally run into, where the existing products are bad.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has only one Caldwell source, his 2022 talk with Michael Seibel, ["Where Do Great Startup Ideas Come From?"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8). Because there are so few sources, he doesn't have a thinking page yet, and he never addresses "safe vs. ambitious" directly.

**How we get there**
1. **The ideas that won looked unsafe at the time.** Caldwell lists the takes people had back then, and admits some were his own. Airbnb: "Renting a room in a house with a host there was like the ultimate unappealing, scary, bad thing that no one wanted to do." (@ [4:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=297s)). Coinbase: "People saw bitcoin as a tiny market, that it was going to crash, that it was a bubble." (@ [9:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=590s)). He also says "Getting a bank deal was impossible." (@ 10:23). If you had filtered for safety, all three would have been dropped.
2. **Founders underestimate their own ideas.** "Even Brian in his YC application didn't really believe in his own idea." (@ [10:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=623s)). The simple version, buying bitcoin "in a non-sketchy way with a debit card… That was enough." (@ 10:56). So the size of the idea isn't a dial you set at the start. Plenty of ideas that look modest turn out to be huge.
3. **Hard isn't a reason to avoid an idea.** Caldwell had set up merchant accounts himself before Stripe existed. He says it "was like applying for a mortgage" and calls building a payments company "gnarly and the opposite of easy in every way." (@ [12:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=754s), 13:08). He was one of Stripe's first hundred beta customers. In this talk, a hard problem with a terrible incumbent is the opportunity.
4. **Applied to your question:** "modest and safe" usually means one of two things. Either the idea has been pre-approved by consensus, which these examples show is unreliable, or it avoids hard problems, which are where he found the value. Neither one improves your odds by his reasoning.

**Why he'd say it**
- He measures ideas by whether the existing options are bad: "Buying bitcoin was something people wanted to do, but all of the options were pretty bad." (@ 8:46)
- Seibel draws the conclusion for both of them: ignore the experts, especially if they won't be users (@ 19:42), and "Don't be discouraged if someone's like, that's a tiny market." (@ 20:16). These are Seibel's lines, not Caldwell's.

**One nuance:** he isn't telling you to go grandiose. The Coinbase story cuts the other way too: a plain, modest promise done well was enough. His answer to your question is that "safe vs. ambitious" is the wrong axis. The axis that matters is real pain plus a 10x improvement.

**What would change his answer:** an idea can look safe because it's easy, or because the space has no incumbent pain. In either case it fails his test outright, since there is nothing bad to be 10x better than.

**Caveats:**
- The vault's profile flags this talk as survivorship. It looks back at three huge winners and leaves out the bold ideas that failed.
- Not in the vault: Caldwell also did a well-known YC video with Seibel on "tarpit ideas". Those are ideas that look easy and appealing, so many founders try them and get stuck. As I recall it, that video also argues against "easy-looking" being a sign of a good idea. The vault doesn't include that source, so I can't quote it. It's worth adding if you want a fuller picture of Caldwell.

**What the vault has from him.** Tan is a member, but his only source is the 2024 Lightcone episode "How YC Was Created" (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY). In it he's mostly hosting and interviewing Jessica Livingston. He has no thinking page. **My guess (low confidence, not in the vault):** He'd probably say yes, it matters, and that you should keep the know-how you build portable. Two weak signals point that way:
- **From memory, not checked against the vault:** Tan has been building heavily with coding agents himself. I believe he published his own Claude Code skills setup as an open-source repo, which treats skill files as personal tooling worth keeping and sharing. I haven't verified this, so check it before relying on it.
- **YC's general lean, mostly Paul Graham's:** the vault's YC thinking favours individuals over organisations. PG says he chose art partly because artists "seemed least at the mercy of organizations" (paulgraham.com essay, `web-76d87c7c2e80`). He also tells people to develop "a habit of working on your own projects" (same essay). Both are PG's words, not Tan's, so they can't stand in for Tan's view.

**What could make the guess wrong:** this is really an employment-law question. Work you build on your employer's time and for their job usually belongs to them under standard IP-assignment clauses, whatever any YC partner thinks. Check your contract before you treat those files as yours to take with you.

**Verdict:** No. Both would tell you to stop building and get it in front of users this week. Seibel's line is "launch something bad quickly". The feature requests aren't a to-do list. Keep the few that address your first users' biggest problem and drop the rest until people are actually using the product.

**Based on:** Seibel's part follows from what he said (high confidence). He never talked about feature-request backlogs or AI coding tools, but his rules on MVP size and launching settle the question. Caldwell's part is low confidence: the vault has only one talk with him (2022, on startup ideas), and he says nothing there about launching or feature requests.

**How we get there**
1. Seibel says an MVP should take weeks, not months: "you should be able to build it fast in weeks, not months" ([Startup School 2019 @ 4:29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=269s)). You're 3 months in, so you're already past the limit he sets.
2. His rule for what goes in: "They should just focus on a small set of initial users and their highest order problems and then ignore the rest until later" ([@ 5:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=303s)). Most of the requests from your calls belong in "the rest".
3. Claude Code makes building cheap, but that doesn't break his rule. His reason for speed was never the cost of building. It's that you learn nothing until a user touches the product: "It's a lot harder to learn from your customers when they don't have a product they can play with" ([@ 10:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=639s)). Cheap building actually makes the trap worse, because the spec can grow faster than you notice.

**Why they'd say it**
- **You've already hit the failure he warns about.** "And so, your three-week plan turns into a three-month plan." ([@ 11:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=704s)) His fix is to write the spec down so it can't quietly grow, then cut it: "Just cut the stuff that clearly isn't important. Um, and if there's no non-important things, start cutting important things." ([@ 12:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=737s))
- **Launch means your first user, not a big release.** "How about launch is when you get any customers." ([@ 10:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=607s)) The people on your calls are your launch. Give them the product now.
- **Requests made on a call are guesses. Use is the real test.** "If you put the thing in front of them and it doesn't solve their problem, you know right away." ([@ 10:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=639s)) He also warns: "It might turn out the full thing that you want to build isn't what your customers want at all." ([@ 3:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=199s))
- **Delay feeds on itself.** "If you don't have anything out in the world, it's very easy to just delay, delay, delay, delay." ([@ 12:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=771s)) He adds: "You'd be surprised at how many founders journeys end before a single user has actually interacted with a product they've created." ([@ 2:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=134s))
- **Don't get attached to what you've built.** "Hold the problem you're solving tightly, hold the customer tightly, hold the solution you're building loosely." ([@ 3:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=199s)) A big feature set you've invested in is exactly what founders fall in love with.
- **Caldwell (my extrapolation):** In the 2022 talk ([Where Do Great Startup Ideas Come From?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8)), he and Seibel make one point that applies here: important features show up through use, not up-front requests. Seibel says Airbnb "didn't realize the insight around facilitating payments ... when they launched", and only found it when Chesky used his own product ([@ 4:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=264s)). Caldwell's lesson from Stripe is about depth for one specific user, not breadth: "They went nuts at making something that developers would just freak out about." ([@ 15:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=918s))

**What they've done:** Seibel points to famous first versions that were thin. Airbnb had no payments and no map. Justin.tv, his own company, had one channel. Stripe had no bank deals, and its founders came to your office to integrate it by hand. "All of these are billion-dollar companies and they all started with something that most people would say is pretty shitty." ([@ 7:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=472s))

**What would change their answer:** Seibel makes one exception, a "heavy MVP" for regulated or hard-tech products where a thin version can't legally or physically ship. Even then, he says, you can start with a website. If a requested feature is the thing that stops your first user from getting any value at all, it goes in. If it's just one more thing someone mentioned on a call, it doesn't.

One limit on all this: Seibel's examples are billion-dollar survivors, so they don't show how many lean MVPs failed.

I looked through the yc-pre vault. **It has nothing from Michael Seibel on cofounder breakups, vesting disputes or lawyers.** His two sources there are about MVPs (2019) and startup ideas (2022). So most of the answer below comes from his general thinking and from what I know of him outside the vault, and I've labeled it that way.

---

**Verdict:** Settle it quickly and cheaply, stop paying lawyers to argue over equity that is probably worth close to nothing, and then decide whether the remaining founder keeps building or you both move on.

**Based on:** mostly beyond the vault (confidence: low to medium)

**What I know of him outside the vault (no quotes from it):**
- He has often said that cofounder fights are one of the most common ways early startups die, and that YC partners spend a lot of their time on these disputes.
- His usual advice is to use standard vesting (4 years with a 1-year cliff) so a departure is handled by the paperwork and not by a fight.
- He tends to say that a pre-product-market-fit company is worth very little. Fighting over percentages of it makes little sense when the startup itself is what's on the line.

**What in the vault points the same way:**
1. **Delay kills.** "If you don't have anything out in the world, it's very easy to just delay, delay, delay, delay." ([2019 talk @ 12:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=771s)) Months of letters between lawyers are exactly that kind of delay. If one of you plans to keep building, that time is gone.
2. **Hold the problem tightly and the solution loosely** ([same talk @ 3:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=199s)). Applied to your case: what matters is whether someone keeps working on the customer's problem, not who ends up with which shares.
3. **This situation is what YC's cofounder advice is meant to prevent.** These quotes are from other YC people, not Seibel. Paul Graham: "Just wait till your interests are opposed and then you'll see." ([2014 @ 5:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=313s)) Jessica Livingston said the thing she looked at most closely in YC interviews was "what was the relationship between the co-founders like?" ([2018 @ 14:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s))

**In practice, the way he'd likely see it:**
- **Check what the documents say.** Under the standard 1-year cliff, nobody has vested anything at 9 months. If your cofounder has "vested a chunk", either there's no cliff, there was acceleration, or the shares were issued without vesting. Your stock purchase agreements decide what he's entitled to. Start from them, not from what either of you thinks is fair.
- **Make a fast deal.** Pre-PMF, a common settlement is that the departing founder keeps what has actually vested and the company repurchases the unvested shares. Sometimes the departing founder gives back a bit more in exchange for a clean release. Get it done in weeks.
- **Decide what happens to the company.** If neither of you would keep working on it without the other, wind it down cleanly. If one of you would, that person needs a cap table that a future investor can accept. A large stake held by a former cofounder who no longer works there makes fundraising harder.

**What would change his answer:** if the company has real traction or real value at stake, or if there was actual misconduct (IP taken, money misused). Then the lawyers are doing necessary work.

---

This is not legal advice. Your lawyers have the documents and know your jurisdiction. The one practical takeaway is to ask both of them what a two-week settlement would look like.

I can't answer this from the vault's Garry Tan material. The vault has nothing from him on AI or agents.

**What the vault actually has from Tan:** he appears in one source, a 2024 podcast episode with Jessica Livingston about how YC was started. His only recorded views there are about fund returns, e.g. "If you funded all of the companies in the batch you would actually create a VC fund that was better than pretty much most of the VC funds returns, period, historically." ([How YC Was Created @ 40:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=2430s)). A raw-text search for "AI" and "agent" across every source found nothing. The vault has no thinking page for him either.

**Verdict (a guess, not his words):** pick one real, painful workflow in your own company and get an agent doing it end-to-end this week. Use it yourself every day and judge it only by whether the work actually gets done. Don't spend the week researching tools.

**Based on:** mostly beyond the vault (confidence: low). Two things support it:

1. **What I know of Tan from outside the vault (not in the vault, so no quotes):** in 2025 he talked publicly about "vibe coding". He said about a quarter of YC's Winter 2025 batch had codebases almost entirely written by AI, and he pushed founders to use these tools hands-on. That points to "go use it" over "go study it".
2. **The nearest YC rule that is in the vault comes from Michael Seibel, not Tan.** Seibel says to put a working product in front of real users fast and judge it by their contact with it: "If you can walk away from one thing from this presentation, it's launch something bad quickly." ([How to Plan an MVP @ 1:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=101s)). He also says to be your own user: "It's even more helpful if you're your own user so you can tell whether your product's working for you." (@ 0:33). Applied to adopting agents: run them on your own real work, start small and rough, and keep it short. Weeks, not months.

**What would change the answer:** if Tan has said something specific about how founders should adopt agents, like which workflows to start with or whether to build or buy, that would replace this guess. The vault doesn't contain it yet.

**To get a real answer**, add Tan's own material to the vault. His @garrytan channel is already set up as a source, and his Lightcone episodes on AI are on the YC channel. The "-pre" vault may also stop before most of his AI-era content. If you want, I can run `wwxd sources yc-pre --status candidate` and list the Tan videos about AI for you to approve.

**Verdict:** PG would keep asking one thing: **who wants this badly today, and how do you know?** He'd want named users, meaning the developers whose agents are trying to buy things right now and failing. Then he'd want your weekly growth among them. "Infrastructure for the agent economy" is the kind of idea he warns sounds plausible because it was thought up rather than lived, so he'd want proof it isn't that.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has nothing from PG about AI agents or agent payments. What follows applies his stated rules to your case.

**How we get there**
1. He thinks the best ideas come from working at the leading edge, not from looking for a market. You should "live in the future" ([yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ @ 29:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1746s)), and ideas you consciously think up tend to be "not only bad, but bad and plausible sounding" ([@ 24:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1474s)).
2. The rule behind it, from his thinking page: something people actually want comes before everything else, and "There is no boss to trick. ... There's only users" ([@ 12:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=730s)).
3. Agent payments fit both halves. It's a real frontier, but "infrastructure for X" is also the classic idea built from a trend instead of from one person's pain. So his first test would be whether you came to it by building agents yourselves and hitting the wall.

**What he'd push you on**
- **Who is the user, exactly?** The agent developer, the merchant, or the person who owns the agent? For a startup, "What you need to know... is expertise in your own users" ([@ 5:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=347s)). He'd want one answer, not three.
- **Are they using it now?** Show the usage graph, not the architecture. "Someone who knows zero about fund raising but has made something users really love will have an easier time raising money. Than someone who knows every trick in the book, but has a flat usage graph." ([@ 13:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=797s))
- **Growth rate, not total volume.** Small numbers are fine. Steer by the weekly rate ([Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)).
- **Do things that don't scale.** Be willing to handle each customer's integration by hand: "pay a ridiculous amount of attention to your tiny initial set of customers" ([superlinear](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). The Stripe-by-hand example is Seibel's ([yt-1hHMwLxN6EM](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM)), but PG states the principle.
- **Why don't existing payment systems already work for agents?** If agents get by today with a stored card and a headless browser, he'd ask what's actually broken. His rule is that a mediocre but popular thing is worth replacing. But he also says "there's often a hidden reason why... Perhaps customers have bad taste or have broken procedures for deciding what to buy" ([superlinear](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). Here the hidden reasons are probably merchants' fraud and bot defences, chargeback liability, and card network rules. He'd want to know which of those you remove and which you're betting will change.
- **Are you playing house?** Protocol specs, partnership announcements and a standards body without paying users are "the outward forms of starting a startup" ([@ 7:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=452s)).

**What would change his answer:** a handful of developers already routing real purchases through you every week, who'd be stuck without you. Then he'd stop asking whether the idea is real and start asking how fast it's growing. He'd also tell you not to worry that the idea looks dumb or too early to investors. That part is mostly Seibel's and Caldwell's point about Stripe and Coinbase ([yt-Jcuqq48CNj8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8)), not PG's.
